t: women and slaves are exempt from Torah study. The exemption for women is learned from the verse cited here, “and you shall teach them to your sons”, excluding your daughters (and see below, halakhah 13). And slaves are exempt from the commandments from which women are exempt (see, for example, Hilchot Keriat Shema 4:1 and others), and in addition it is forbidden for a person to teach his slave Torah (Hilchot Avadim 8:18).
for whoever is obligated to learn is obligated to teach. Therefore one who is not obligated to learn is not obligated to teach.
his grandson. His son's son.
from the oral tradition. The Sages' tradition of interpreting the verses.
“and the sons of the prophets went out”. There it speaks of disciples of the prophets, not literal sons, from which we learn that students too may be called “sons.”
why was he commanded about his son and his grandson. Why was he commanded about them specially, since he is obligated to teach all students.
to give priority to his son over his grandson. To give priority to his sons over his grandchildren, and to them over others.
and he is obligated to hire a teacher for his son. Not only is he obligated to teach his son himself, he is even obligated to pay money to have him taught (and see below, halakhah 7).
and he is not obligated to teach his fellow's son except for free. He is not obligated to spend money for him.
he is obligated to teach himself when he recognizes it. When he comes to the awareness that he is obligated to study.
“and you shall learn them and take care to do them”. One must study Torah in order to keep and perform its commandments, as will be explained below.
for study precedes action. It is more important than it (and see below 3:3).
for study brings to action. For only if study precedes the performance of commandments will he know what he must do and how to perform the commandments.
and action does not bring to study. For Torah study is not the result of performing the commandments.

he takes precedence over his son. If they do not have enough resources for both to study, because the commandment for himself takes precedence over his commandment toward others (and see above, halakhah 1).
discerning and understanding what he will learn more than he. That the son is more successful in his studies than the father.
he should not neglect it. But should study as much as he can.
his mind is not free to study. Because from the time he marries his mind is occupied with providing for the household (Hilchot Ishut 15:2).
and if his inclination overpowers him, etc.. With thoughts of desire, which makes study difficult (see there 15:3).
from when does his father begin to teach him Torah. The young son.
from when he begins to speak he teaches him “Moses commanded us Torah,” etc.. To implant in his heart faith in the importance of the Torah and in the unity of God.
according to his health. According to the child's state of health; if he is weak, one must wait until he grows more (see below 2:2).
the Written Torah, all of it. All the books of Tanakh.
“See, I have taught you,” etc.. These are Moses' words to Israel about having taught them the Torah as the Lord taught him.
for free. Without payment of a fee.
he should learn for pay, etc.. That in such a case one must pay a fee.
may he teach others for pay. Is he permitted to teach for pay if he himself studied for pay?
a poor man who goes door to door. A beggar.
one with a wife and children. Whom he is obligated to support (see above, halakhah 5).
by day and by night. Every day and every night.
“and you shall meditate on it day and night”. And the beginning of the verse: “This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth.”
and nevertheless they engaged in Torah day and night. Their hard labor or physical limitation did not prevent them from engaging in Torah as a mitzvah.

and they are among those who transmitted the tradition, each from the mouth of another, from the mouth of Moses our teacher. Those Sages are counted in the chain of tradition transmitting the Oral Torah (see the Introduction to the Mishneh Torah).
“lest they depart from your heart”. That you not forget them.
to divide into three. To divide into three parts.
he will understand and comprehend the end of a matter from its beginning. He will know how to deduce the consequences of the laws from the study of the verses.
and derive one thing from another, etc.. By methods of inference and analogy.
and judge by the rules by which the Torah is expounded. He will use the various methods of expounding verses accepted from the Sages.
how is the essence of the rules. What are the principles on which the rules are built.

and how he derives the forbidden and the permitted and the like from the things he learned from the oral tradition. That he knows how to derive the halakhah from discussion of what he received from his teachers by tradition.
and he engaged in labor three hours a day and in Torah nine. On the importance of engaging in a trade alongside study, see below 3:9-10.
and the words of the tradition are included in the Written Torah. Prophets and Writings are also among the written books.
and their explanation is included in the Oral Torah. The explanations of Scripture, which are also among the things transmitted by tradition.

and the subjects called Pardes are included in Talmud. Contemplation of God's existence and greatness (see Hilchot Yesodei ha-Torah 4:13), whose subject too is understanding how things derive from their source.
at the beginning of a person's study. When he is not yet versed in the Written and Oral Torah.
at fixed times. Set times.
a woman who studied Torah. Who is permitted to observe even commandments that she is not obligated in (see Hilchot Tzitzit 3:9).
the Sages commanded that a person not teach his daughter. Although if she studied she has reward, one should not teach her in the first instance the way one does with sons.
and they turn words of Torah into nonsense. They may misunderstand the words of Torah and use them for vain talk.
tiflut. Something worthless. Others explain: something improper.
in the Oral Torah. Where there is more room for misunderstanding and distortion.
in every province and every district. In every city and every region.
they place the people of the city under cherem. They punish them with cherem (for the meaning of the punishment see below chapter 7).
they lay waste the city. For it has no right to exist.
according to the strength of the son and the build of his body. According to the child's physical ability (above 1:6).
and the teacher strikes them. He is permitted to strike them (and see Hilchot Rotze'ach 5:6).
the blow of an enemy, the chastisement of the cruel. Great suffering (based on Jeremiah 30:14).
in order to train them to study day and night. Which is the obligation of study (above 1:8).
at the end of the day. That they finish early, before the Sabbath or festival begins.
and on festivals. Because of the joy of the festival.
they do not read in the first instance. That is, in something new they have not yet read, for this impairs the rest of the Sabbath.
but they review the first. They repeat what they already learned on a weekday.
and even for the building of the Temple. For the study of children is more important than it, since it sustains the world (above, halakhah 1; and see also Hilchot Beit ha-Bechirah 1:12).
for he leaves the children and goes out. And does not watch over their studies the whole time.
does other work with them. While teaching.
is lax in teaching them. He does not teach them enough, or teaches them with errors (see also Hilchot Sechirut 10:7).
“cursed be he who does the Lord's work deceitfully”. One who does not faithfully fulfill his mission to teach the Torah of the Lord.
a man of fear. God-fearing, who will be careful in his work.
quick to read and to be precise. An expert in reading and its grammar.
because of their mothers, etc.. And he turns out to be flirting with women (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 22:13).
because of their fathers. And they turn out to be secluded with her (ibid.).
learn with one teacher. This is the maximum number of students for one teacher.
they appoint two teachers of children for them. And divide them into two groups.
to another teacher who is quicker than he. To a teacher more expert than the first, since there is benefit in this for the child's learning.
in what case is this said, etc.. This permission is limited to cases where there is no danger to the child as a result of the transfer.
a sturdy building. A strong structure.
an alley. A small street.
to become a teacher. To engage in this profession, and children will come to his house and cause noise and commotion.
even one of the residents of the courtyard. For the neighbors are present in the same courtyard as the teacher, and the source of noise is adjacent to their houses.
his neighbors cannot protest. For this is permitted to him, as follows (see Hilchot Shekhenim 6:12).
he cannot protest. He cannot claim that the other is robbing him of his livelihood (see there, halakhah 8).

“The Lord was pleased, for His righteousness' sake, to magnify Torah and make it glorious”. The Lord desires, because of His righteousness, to magnify the Torah and spread it. And the more teachers of children there are, the more the spread of Torah will grow.
with three crowns. Three special distinctions.
the crown of priesthood Aaron merited... the crown of kingship David merited. And each of them is an inheritance for his descendants alone (see Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:1-2, Hilchot Melachim 1:7).
an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob. For the Torah is an inheritance for all of Israel, and not for a particular tribe or family (see Hilchot Melachim 8:10).
“By me kings reign... by me princes rule”. For kingship and authority depend only on wisdom, which is the Torah.
a mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over an ignoramus high priest. Although in terms of family lineage their standing is reversed (see also Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:17-18).

“she is more precious than pearls”. Wisdom, which is the Torah, is more honored than pearls. And the homiletical interpretation is based on the spelling “mi-peninim”, read as “lifnei lifnim” (Rabbi Kafih's note on the Commentary on the Mishnah, end of Horayot).
who entered the innermost. The Holy of Holies, which the high priest enters once a year on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Avodat Yom ha-Kippurim chapter 4).
is equal to Torah study. Is equal in value to Torah study.
for study brings to action. And for this reason all the commandments depend on Torah study (see above 1:3).
study precedes action everywhere. Torah study takes precedence over fulfilling other commandments.
if the mitzvah can be done by others. Who are not studying, then both will be fulfilled, the study and the mitzvah.
and if not, he does the mitzvah and returns to his Torah. For if he does not fulfill it, he would be nullifying the mitzvah entirely, and this is not “study that brings to action.”
the first judgment of a person. When he is judged for his deeds, after his life.
even not for its own sake. Not out of love of God but in order to receive reward (see Hilchot Teshuvah 10:4-5).

for from not for its own sake he comes to for its own sake. Through becoming accustomed to the words of the Torah, he grows wise and understands that it is fitting to study it for its own sake and not for another benefit (see also Hilchot Teshuvah 10:5).
one whose heart moved him. Who volunteered of his own will.
this is the way of the Torah, etc.. That one must toil in it even in physical hardship (see further below, halakhot 7-8).
and the reward is according to the pain. The size of the reward is determined in proportion to the amount of toil.
until I gather money and return and study, etc.. I will wait until I earn money, and then I will study.
you will never merit the crown of Torah. For Torah study will always be pushed aside for other things.
fixed. The central, permanent matter.
casual. Marginal and secondary.
“It is not in heaven,” etc.. The Torah is found neither in heaven nor across the sea, but “the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart to do it” (Deuteronomy 30:14).
it is not found among the arrogant. For heaven alludes to arrogance and haughtiness.
nor among those who cross the sea. This alludes to traveling to a distant land for trade.
not everyone who increases trade becomes wise. For the Torah is not found in him.
do little business and engage in Torah. It is fitting not to pursue money but to be content with one's lot (Hilchot De'ot 2:7).
“Ho, all who are thirsty, come to the waters”. In this parable the prophet calls to go and listen to the words of the Lord, which are the words of the Torah.
flowing. Flowing.
eshboren. A sunken place.
who is covered in the dust of the Sages' feet. Who sits on the ground before them to hear their words (see Hilchot De'ot 6:2).
and the pleasures of time. Things that are passing pleasure.
for his needs, etc.. As much as is needed to sustain himself.
one who takes to heart. Who thinks.
he has desecrated the Name, etc.. For the Torah becomes like any trade by which people earn a living.
“do not make them a crown with which to magnify yourself”. Not to make them like a crown with which to be honored.
“nor a spade with which to dig”. Not to make it a means of obtaining monetary benefit.
love work and hate rabbinic office. To earn a living from work and not from authority.
and any Torah without work ends up neglected, etc.. Because of the inability to earn a living.
a robber. A bandit.
and it is the way of the early pious ones. For so the great Sages of Israel behaved in ancient times (see above 1:9).
happy are you in this world. That you have the means to earn a living.
and it is good for you in the World to Come. For that is the time of the reward of the commandments (Hilchot Teshuvah 8:1).
who is lax. Who engages in them half-heartedly.
“I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids”. He will sleep little (based on Psalms 132:4).
by way of allusion. That the matter is alluded to by this verse, though it is not its simple meaning.
“if you are slack on the day of distress, your strength is small”. That if you grow slack from the Torah, then your strength will not stand by you in days of distress.
for I learned it with effort. With exertion.
a covenant cut. An absolute promise.
that it is a mitzvah to learn by day and by night. Above 1:8.
and words of wisdom. Words of thought.
the threshing floor of the Torah. The threshing floor is the place for gathering agricultural produce.
“sing in the night”. For Torah study is called song and singing.
a thread of grace. A special charm that illuminates his face.
“By day the Lord commands His kindness, and at night His song is with me”. The Lord's kindness is evident on the face of one who engages in Torah at night.
who paid no attention at all to words of Torah. Who did not care at all about the Torah.

whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will in the end neglect it in poverty. One who does not study in his time of wealth will eventually be forced to neglect it because of the preoccupations of poverty.
and whoever fulfills the Torah in poverty will in the end fulfill it in wealth. If he studies Torah even while poor, he will eventually merit reward and wealth.
“because you did not serve, etc.”. The punishments stated in the passage will come upon Israel because they did not serve the Lord when they had an abundance of good.
“that He might humble you and test you, to do you good in your end”. That the purpose of the hardships is only to test, in order to bring about an end of good and wealth for those who withstand it.
in a margemah. According to this homily, interpreted as a place where stones are customarily thrown (Mercurius).
“the wise shall inherit honor”. The Torah is the inheritance of the wise, who walk in the straight path (see Hilchot De'ot 1:4-5).
and all the people need him. For his knowledge of Torah.
the teacher is like an angel of the Lord of hosts. In terms of his conduct.
to a worthy student, pleasant in his deeds. One of good character and good deeds.
or to an innocent one. Whose conduct is not known.
threw a stone at Mercurius. For that is the way this idol is worshiped (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:2).
surrounded by a crown. In a circle around him.
and at first the teacher would sit, etc.. In very ancient times.
and from before the destruction of the Second Temple they practiced, etc.. From this period on, they instituted that all sit during study, so that they not tire.
teaches from his mouth. Himself.
teaches through a translator. Who will relay the teacher's words aloud to the many.
and the teacher should not raise his voice louder than the voice of the translator. Out of respect for the translator.
and the translator should not raise his voice, etc.. Out of respect for the teacher (similarly see Hilchot Tefillah 12:11).
neither to reduce, nor to add, nor to change. The words the teacher said, but he must relay them exactly as they were said.
unless the translator was a Sage's father or his teacher. In which case the translator is permitted to change and add, since he is greater than the Sage.

the teacher said to the translator, “Thus my teacher said to me,” etc.. And he omitted the name of his teacher or father because he is forbidden to call them by it (below 5:5, Hilchot Mamrim 6:3), and the translator is permitted to mention their names.
our teacher. Our master.
until they understand the depth of the halakhah. The teacher is obligated to teach them until they thoroughly understand the reasons for the halakhah.
and my mind is short. It does not grasp the matter.
he is ashamed before his companions, etc.. He is ashamed before others who learned faster than he, and therefore does not say that he did not understand.
he turns out to go in and out of the study hall and learns nothing. For he appears as if he learned and understood, while this is not true.
the bashful does not learn. He does not succeed in learning, because he is ashamed to ask.
nor does the irritable teach. The short-tempered does not succeed in teaching, because the students tell him they understood so that he not be angry at them, even if they did not understand.
in what case is this said. That the teacher should not get angry at students who did not understand.
because of its depth. Because the subject is intricate and complex.
are lax in words of Torah and slack in them. They engage in them without the proper effort (see above 3:12).
and to shame them with words. To rebuke them for their behavior.
in order to sharpen them. To cause them to be precise in their study and understand well what is learned.
cast fear among the students. Cast awe upon them.
levity. Lack of seriousness.
one does not ask the teacher, etc.. These rules are meant so that the questions be to the point and the answers be given with patience and consideration.
to mislead the students, etc.. To ask them misleading questions or perform acts that contradict what they learned, in order to test whether they understood properly.
in order to spur them. To cause them to study other matters.
standing. While standing.
from behind the elders. When a row of Sages hides the teacher.
except on the subject. That they are engaged in.
they attend to the subject. They address this question, since he asked about the subject of study.
they attend to the practical. Practical halakhah, whose importance is greater than something that is not practical.
midrash. Close reading of the verses of the Torah to derive halakhot from them, which is less important than halakhah and greater than aggadah.
and aggadah. Moral teachings derived from the verses or learned from parables and events.
a fortiori and gezerah shavah. Methods of comparison used in the Sages' midrash. A fortiori reasoning rests on logical consideration, whereas gezerah shavah rests on verbal identity in Scripture.
the authority is in the translator's hand from now on. To decide what to ask first, since the translator is the one who asks the teacher himself (above, halakhah 3).
his wisdom is made into shreds. He does not remember a single complete halakhah.
“and slumber will clothe one in rags”. One who is lazy and sleeps will end up wearing torn clothes.

and the sanctity of the study hall is more severe than the sanctity of synagogues. Because of the frequency of study in it, and therefore one may not convert a study hall into a synagogue (Hilchot Tefillah 11:14; and see there 8:3).
is commanded about honoring his father and fearing him. This is the commandment of honoring father and mother (see Hilchot Mamrim chapter 6).

and his teacher more than his father. For his teacher takes precedence over his father in all matters of honor and fear, as will be explained (and in all the laws here it speaks of his primary teacher, as explained below, halakhah 9).
that of his teacher takes precedence over that of his father. He should return his teacher's lost item and afterward deal with his father's.
leaves his teacher's. He helps him unload his burden.

and if his father was a Torah scholar, he redeems his father first. Because of the suffering of captivity and the fact that he is a Torah scholar, he redeems him first and afterward redeems his teacher (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:17-18).

and likewise if his father was a Sage. Who was at the level of a Sage (greater than the category of Torah scholar), out of honor for the Torah he returns his lost item first (compare Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 12:2, where it speaks of a case where it is impossible to return to both; Yad Peshutah).
“when they strove against the Lord”. Said of the congregation of Korach, who disputed the leadership of Moses our teacher.

“which the children of Israel strove with the Lord”. Said in the summary of the sin at the waters of Meribah, where the children of Israel quarreled with Moses over the lack of water: “and the people quarreled with Moses” (Numbers 20:3).

“your complaints are not against us but against the Lord”. Moses' words to the children of Israel after they complained about the shortage of food: “and the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness” (Exodus 16:3).

“and the people spoke against God and against Moses”. Said after the people grew impatient while going around the land of Edom, and complained: “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread and no water, and we loathe this miserable bread” (Numbers 21:5).
who establishes a study session for himself. Who founds a yeshiva in which he teaches regularly.
and his teacher is alive. Still living.
and it is forbidden for a person to rule in front of his teacher ever. To issue halakhic rulings in his teacher's area, even without establishing a yeshiva, for this is brazenness.
twelve mil. A great distance, about twelve kilometers, and it is no longer considered within his territory (see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 20:9).
it is permitted to answer. Whatever is incidental and he has already been asked.
and to separate from the forbidden. To warn a person not to commit a transgression.
for there is a desecration of the Name. In an act of transgression.
something that happened by chance. That occurred by chance.
even if he is at the end of the world etc.. As above 5:2.
a student who has reached the level of ruling. One who understands the ways of halakhah, and rules with deliberation and fear of Heaven.
for she has cast down many slain. Because of the arrogance in him, he rules improperly and causes others to stumble into sin.
and mighty are all her slain. Even if he did not cause them to stumble actively, the result of his refusal to rule is that people stumble into sin (see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 20:8).
they seek to make themselves great before the ignorant and among the people of their city. They want those people to think that they are great and learned in Torah.
to call his teacher by his name. By his personal name.
to call others who have the same name as his teacher. It is forbidden even to call others who bear the same name as his teacher; rather, he calls them by a different name.
as he does with his father's name. That he must change it when calling others (Hilchot Mamrim 6:3).

provided that the name is unusual. If the name is rare and distinctive, then using it shows disrespect to his teacher or his father. But if it is a common name, it is permitted to call others by it not in his presence (ibid.).
as friends give to one another. Companions, without ceremonial honor.
bows. Bends over in submission.
he should not remove his tefillin in front of his teacher. Because this is a casting off of the yoke.
and he should not recline. To eat reclining in the manner of dignity (see Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 7:8).
and he should not pray in front of his teacher etc.. For all of these involve arrogance.
and he should not enter the bathhouse with his teacher. Because this is not a respectful way (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:16).
in his teacher's place. In the place where he usually sits.
and he should not decide matters in his presence. In a matter that is to be decided by reasoning, it is forbidden to say otherwise than what the teacher said (see Responsa of the Rambam, no. 264).
he should not turn his back to him. He should not turn his back toward him.
he backs away. Withdraws walking backward (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:4, Hilchot Tefillah 9:2).
as far as his eyes can see etc.. As long as he sees him (compare below 6:6).
to greet his teacher on the festival. To go visit him on the three pilgrimage festivals, for greeting one's teacher is equal to greeting the Divine Presence, and it is like a pilgrimage.
tasks that a slave does for his master. Of service and attendance.

and he is concerned that they will say, he is a slave. He is concerned that because he serves the teacher, people will think he is his slave, and this would harm his lineage. If he were wearing tefillin there would be no cause for concern, since slaves do not wear tefillin (Hilchot Tefillin 4:13, Hilchot Kriyat Shema 4:1; and compare Hilchot Avadim 8:17).
he does not put on his shoes or take them off. For these are tasks specific to a Canaanite slave (Hilchot Avadim 1:7).
he says to him, "Our teacher, you taught us thus and so". As if he is asking him and not warning him (Hilchot Mamrim 6:11).
and he should not say... until he mentions the name of the one who said it. That he should not say them in front of others, so that they do not mistakenly attribute the words to his teacher.
he tears all his garments etc.. As with one who mourns for his father and mother (Hilchot Evel 8:3, 9:5).
and he never mends it. It is forbidden to sew the tear in a way that the garment looks whole as before (see Hilchot Evel 9:1-3).
but he stands before him. When he is present beside him (below 6:1).
just as he tears for all the dead etc.. His other relatives, for whom the tearing is less than that for his father and mother (see Hilchot Evel 8:2).
he stands before him and tears for him. Like a student-colleague.
whose character traits are well-directed. Whose traits are refined (see Hilchot De'ot 1:4).
even though he did not learn anything from him. For this is not by the law of honoring one's teacher, but a manner of proper conduct.
to forgo his honor. That they not honor him with the things listed in this chapter.
to honor him. To honor him like any Torah scholar (below 6:1).
for they are the children who benefit in this world and in the World to Come. See above 1:2.
they increase the teacher's wisdom and broaden his heart. They benefit his learning and develop his intellect.
until he draws out of him, through his questions, glorious wisdom. Thanks to the students' questions, the teacher arrives at precision in his words and at making them clear.
to honor him. To honor him and rise before him, as below.
an elder (zaken) is one who has acquired wisdom. "Zaken" means a wise person, and the word "zaken" is expounded as an acronym: "zeh kanah" (this one acquired).
once he comes within four cubits of him. At that point it is evident that the rising is in honor of that sage.
until he passes from in front of him. And he is no longer facing him (see further detail below, halakhah 6).
not in the bathhouse... rising that includes honor. These are not dignified places where it is fitting to honor a person.
craftsmen. Tradesmen, who if they rose before the sage would stop work, causing a monetary loss.
what kind of honor is it that involves no monetary loss. For honor does not involve a financial loss.
he closes his eyes to the sage. Deliberately so as not to see him, and not be obligated to stand before him.
a matter entrusted to the heart. For it cannot be proven whether he saw or did not see; only the person himself knows.
that he would trouble the people and arrange himself toward them. That he would cause them trouble by walking among them deliberately, when another option exists.
he should take a short route. The shortest route.
and the sages would go around etc.. For it is a measure of piety to walk even a longer way so as not to trouble others.
riding. If the sage is not walking but riding an animal.
three who were walking on the road. If the sage is walking on the road and two accompany him, they honor him by walking in this manner.
until he reaches four cubits from him. This is the law of honor for any sage (above, halakhah 1).
the head of the court. The head of the court, who is a kind of deputy to the nasi of the Sanhedrin (Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:3).
if he saw the nasi standing before him as far as his eyes can see. Similar to his primary teacher, above 5:7.
and a nasi who forwent his honor. And agrees that they not honor him so much (and see above 5:11).
enters. The study hall.
they make two rows for him, standing on this side and that. Those beside whom he passes.
when the public needs them. And therefore they must enter the study hall.

they may leap over the heads of the people. They are permitted to step between the seated people, even though it looks as if they are walking over their heads, and those people need not stand before them.
and it is no praise for a Torah scholar to enter last. For this is not proper conduct; he should be among those who arrive early at the study hall.
who have the understanding to listen. Who understand and are able to learn.
they turn their faces toward their father. They sit facing him, like all the students.
they lack the understanding to listen. If they are unable to learn.
they turn their faces toward the people. So that it is seen that they sit there out of respect for their father but not as learners.

he may not stand... so that his honor not exceed the honor of Heaven. Since people accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven twice a day, in the recitation of the Shema (Hilchot Kriyat Shema 1:1-2), they ruled that he should stand in this manner only twice.
very old. Very elderly.
a sage who is a youth. Great in Torah but young in years.
only to honor him. It suffices that he straighten up slightly in a way that shows he is honoring him.
they honor him with words. They honor him with words of praise.
to support him. That he lean on it, which is a respectful manner.

they do not go out to work with their own persons... so that they not be degraded before the ignorant. For if they went out to work with their own bodies, the ignorant would think Torah scholars are equal to them in status (but if money is collected, it is also collected from Torah scholars - Hilchot Shecheinim 6:6).
for the building of walls etc.. The needs of guarding the city (see ibid. 6:4-6).
for the king's tribute. A gift that the public must give to the king.

Even though they give among the nations, now I will gather them, and they shall begin to diminish a little from the burden of king and princes. The Sages expounded this verse: those who study ("yitnu") halakhot will be exempted ("vayachelu") from paying taxes ("masa melekh vesarim").
they let him sell first. They give him the exclusive right to sell that merchandise, and only afterward allow other people.
and he was among many litigants. For there are many seeking judgment (on the order of precedence in judgment, see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 21:6).
and they seat him. Even though litigants normally stand (see ibid. 21:3-4).

and they mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets. This verse is part of a passage listing the sins of the king of Judah, the officers and the people, and explains why the wrath of the Lord rose against Israel, until He brought up the king of Babylon to destroy the Temple and Jerusalem.

if you reject My statutes... because he has despised the word of the Lord. For the attitude toward the sages parallels the attitude toward God's statutes and words, because the sages teach the words of God.
he has no share. In the World to Come.
if witnesses came that he had insulted him. And so the matter became known to the court.
excommunication (niddui). The laws of niddui will be explained below, chapter 7.
a litra of gold. A large sum, as payment for humiliation (see Hilchot Chovel 3:5-6).
everywhere. Even outside the Land of Israel, where fines are not adjudicated (Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8-9), since this is not a fine but payment for his humiliation.
and they release him when he repents. They lift the niddui if the one who insulted repented.
until the one for whose sake they excommunicated him is appeased. Until the person who insulted appeases the sage (some vocalize "ad sheyiretzeh," meaning until the sage agrees to lift the niddui).
who was insolent toward him. Who acted brazenly toward him.
and if the sage wished to forgive him. To waive his honor from the outset and ignore the insolence (and see below 7:13, Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:6).
all his students are obligated to treat the excommunicate with niddui. For they are obligated in honor of the teacher.
all the people. Who are obligated in honoring Torah scholars.
and likewise one excommunicated for the nasi is excommunicated for all Israel etc.. For all are obligated in his honor (above, halakhah 6), but he is not obligated in theirs.
excommunicated by his town. That he was excommunicated for the sake of the honor of the town's sages.
one who insults a sage. Above, halakhot 12-14.
one who insults an agent of the court. Hilchot Sanhedrin 25:5.
one who calls his fellow a slave. See Hilchot Teshuvah 3:14.
one whom the court sent for and set a time for, and he did not come. Hilchot Sanhedrin 25:8.
one who did not accept the judgment upon himself. Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 22:3, Hilchot To'ein VeNit'an 1:5, Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:17, 25:11.
a vicious dog. Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:9.
or a rickety ladder. Hilchot Rotzeach 11:4.
one who sells his land to a gentile. Hilchot Shecheinim 12:7.
one who testifies against a Jew in gentile courts. Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:7.
a butcher who is a kohen and does not separate the priestly gifts. Hilchot Bikkurim 9:9.
one who desecrates the second day of a festival in the Diaspora. Hilchot Yom Tov 1:22.
one who works on the eve of Pesach after midday. Ibid. 8:17.
one who mentions the name of Heaven in vain. Hilchot Shevu'ot 12:9-11.
one who brings the public to eat sacred offerings outside. Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 8:11.
one who calculates years and fixes months outside the Land. Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 1:8.
one who causes the blind to stumble. Hilchot Rotzeach 12:14; and see Hilchot Mamrim 6:9.
one who prevents the public from performing a commandment. Hilchot Teshuvah 4:1.
a butcher from whose hand a treifah came out. Hilchot Shechitah 10:14, Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 8:9.
a butcher who did not check his knife before a sage. Hilchot Shechitah 1:26.
one who hardens himself to know. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:18-19.
one who divorced his wife etc.. Ibid. 21:27.
a sage with a bad reputation. See below 7:1.
one who excommunicates someone not liable to niddui. Who uses the power of niddui improperly.
they never excommunicate him publicly. Because of the desecration of God's name this would involve.

unless he acted like Jeroboam son of Nebat and his companions. Who sinned and caused the public to sin (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:10; and see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:21 regarding removing a person from his position when he rebels).
they flog him discreetly. Without publicity.
be honored and stay at home. Preserve your dignity and stay at home, and do not come into contact with anyone (based on II Kings 14:10).
it is forbidden for the court to rush and excommunicate him quickly. Hastily and without having deliberated the matter.
even if they are counting votes to flog him. Which is a Torah obligation.
if he became liable to flogging. See Hilchot Sanhedrin chapters 16-19.
rebellion lashes (makkat mardut). Lashes for transgressions that are of rabbinic origin.
they count votes to strike him. For they refrain only from niddui.
and how is the niddui performed. The wording of the declaration that the one excommunicating says.
shamta. The Aramaic term for niddui.
and the cherem. More severe than niddui (explained below, halakhah 5).

and cursed, with an oath, with a curse, with niddui. The word "arur" (cursed) can serve as an expression of a curse or an oath, and also as an expression of niddui (see Hilchot Shevu'ot 2:2, Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:3).
resides. Is permitted.
the practice that the excommunicate should follow. How he should behave and what is forbidden to him.
to cut his hair and launder like a mourner. To have his hair cut and launder his clothes, as the law of a mourner (see Hilchot Evel 5:1-3).
and they do not invite others to say the Grace together because of him. They do not count him toward the zimun for Grace after Meals with three.
and they do not sit with him within four cubits. For they separate from him.
he teaches others and others teach him. He teaches them Torah and they teach him.
and he hires and is hired. As a laborer for work.
that is, they stone him etc.. As an expression that he deserved to be stoned.
they do not eulogize him and do not accompany his bier. They do not honor him in any way.
more than that. There are additional laws of distancing applying to him, beyond those of the excommunicate.
only a little business for his livelihood. In an amount sufficient for his subsistence.
thirty days. The period of the niddui (and see also Hilchot To'ein VeNit'an 1:5, Hilchot Sanhedrin 25:11).
by three, even laymen. Ordinary people. The lifting of the niddui is done after the excommunicate has retracted his conduct (below, halakhot 9 and 13; and above 6:12).
or an expert individual. A sage proficient in the laws of the Torah (see Hilchot Shevu'ot 6:1).
and a student may release... even in the place of the teacher. He may do so, though regarding vows and oaths he may release only with his teacher's consent (ibid. 6:3).
three others come and release him. They may lift the niddui for him, and it is not necessary that those who excommunicated him release him.
one who does not know who excommunicated him. Who does not recognize the one who excommunicated him, and therefore cannot go to him to have the niddui lifted.
a conditional niddui. One that was made conditional on something that will happen or be done.
even from his own mouth. Where a person said of himself that he would be excommunicated on a certain condition.
requires annulment (hafarah). Whether or not the condition was fulfilled.
with the consent of so-and-so. On the condition that a certain sage agrees to that niddui.
a matter for which one is liable to niddui. Explained above 6:14.
one who was excommunicated in a dream. In such a case there is cause to be concerned that Heaven is hinting to him that he is rebuked, and he must receive correction and release.
people who recite halakhot. Who drill established halakhot.
up to a parsah. A distance of about four kilometers, which is a person's boundary.
even three may release him. For this release is only a request that Heaven have mercy on him.
and there is nothing between niddui and annulment. It is possible that there be no interval of time between them.
to leave this one in his niddui. To leave that person excommunicated.
to place this one under cherem from the outset. To decree a cherem on him immediately, without his having been under niddui first (see above, halakhah 6).
and to place under cherem one who eats with him etc.. Restrictions that make the usual laws of cherem more stringent.
and to make a fence for the Torah so that sinners not breach it. To fortify the laws of the Torah, so that sinners do not damage them.
it is not praiseworthy. This is not proper conduct.
also do not pay attention to all the words that they speak. Do not take to heart all the bad things that others say about you.
they hear their disgrace and do not answer. They do not respond to one who tries to hurt them.
and this is the way of Torah scholars, in which it is fitting to walk. Not to be strict about one's own honor and to stay far from the trait of anger (see Hilchot De'ot 2:3, 5:13).
publicly. Before the public.
it is forbidden for him to forgo his honor. For the honor of the Torah is thereby degraded in the eyes of the public.
*. In the printed edition they skipped the letter het in the numbering of the halakhot.
